cases.name: zip-slip-basic
cases.why: CVE-2026-27800's canonical shape: a member name that simply walks out of the destination.

cases.name: zip-slip-nested
cases.why: The same escape, buried under plausible-looking directories and over-popped, so a check that only inspects the first component or the leaf sails past it.

cases.name: zip-absolute-member
cases.why: An anchored member. Nothing is popped and no `..` appears, so a traversal-only filter waves it through and the join yields /etc/passwd.

cases.name: zip-backslash-traversal
cases.why: A Windows-authored (spec-violating) name. On Windows it is a traversal; on Unix it is one legal filename — the exact shape that makes an extractor safe on the developer's machine and not on the user's, so it is refused on both.

cases.name: zip-drive-qualified-member
cases.why: A drive qualifier is anchored without being rooted, and Path.Combine would discard the destination entirely when it met one.

cases.name: zip-verbatim-prefix-member
cases.why: The \\?\ prefix bypasses Win32 path normalization, so a name sanitized by a normalizing check can be un-sanitized by prefixing it.

cases.name: zip-dot-file-member
cases.why: A file member whose name reduces to nothing would have to overwrite the destination root itself with a file. Contained, and still nonsense.

cases.name: zip-duplicate-member
cases.why: Two members at one path. The second would overwrite the first — a payload smuggled past a reviewer who read the first copy, and a write the rollback could never undo.

cases.name: zip-member-count-cap
cases.why: An archive that declares more members than the caller allows. The cap is charged per member read, so it trips on the fourth rather than after the whole archive is walked.

cases.name: zip-bomb-member
cases.why: 32 MiB of zeros in a ~32 KiB archive, tripping the SHIPPED per-member default rather than a value the case tightened for itself. Nothing is buffered: the cap is enforced against bytes counted as they leave the decompressor.

cases.name: zip-bomb-total
cases.why: Every member sits comfortably under the per-member cap; together they do not. A cap on one member alone is not a cap.

cases.name: zip-partial-then-escape
cases.why: The rollback case. Three innocent members land on disk first and a traversal follows, so a green result here means the extraction was genuinely unwound rather than merely stopped.

cases.name: zip-member-under-a-pre-existing-symlink
cases.why: CVE-2026-27976's write-through, at the filesystem level: the member name is impeccable and the link is already there. Only resolving against the live filesystem catches this, which is why the syntactic filter is a pre-filter and not the check.

cases.name: zip-symlink-member
cases.why: A zip has no member-type field, so a Unix-authored archive declares a symlink in the HIGH sixteen bits of the external attributes (S_IFLNK | 0777) and writes the target as the member's body. Nothing escapes today — this extractor cannot create a link, so it would write an ordinary file whose CONTENT is an outside path — but the class documents 'link members are refused wholesale' with no format caveat, and a downstream re-packer handed that file resurrects the link.

cases.name: zip-symlink-then-write-through
cases.why: CVE-2026-27976's shape in the OTHER container. Member 1 declares an in-root symlink pointing outside; member 2 has a blameless name and would be written through it by an extractor that honoured the link. Refusing link members kills it at member 1 — and before that refusal existed member 1 was written as a plain file, which made member 2 fail with a DESTINATION-unusable error, a reason that told the caller nothing about what the archive was doing.

cases.name: zip-container-size-cap
cases.why: The container cap, charged before ZipArchive reads a byte. It is the only cap that can be enforced ahead of the central directory — which ZipArchive materializes in full before handing back the first member, so the per-member caps cannot bound what a 200k-entry directory costs to parse.

cases.name: zip-benign
cases.why: The gate that only ever rejects proves nothing. A plain archive must come out whole, with an implicit parent directory created for a nested member and an explicit directory member honoured.

cases.name: tar-slip-basic
cases.why: Zip Slip is not a zip problem. The tar reader is a second code path and gets the same filter.

cases.name: tar-absolute-member
cases.why: GNU tar strips a leading slash on write and warns; nothing obliges an attacker's tar to.

cases.name: tar-symlink-escape
cases.why: A symlink member aimed straight out of the destination. Refused as a link member before its target is ever considered, which is why this case can name /etc without depending on /etc existing.

cases.name: tar-symlink-then-write-through
cases.why: CVE-2026-27976 itself, and the most important row here. Member 1 plants an in-root symlink pointing outside; member 2 has a blameless name and writes through it. Refusing link members kills it at member 1 — and the pre-existing-symlink case proves member 2 would have been refused too.

cases.name: tar-hardlink-escape
cases.why: A hard link aliases an existing inode under a second name — no symlink involved, so a symlink-only check misses it entirely.

cases.name: tar-fifo-member
cases.why: A member that is not a file, a directory or a link. Nothing an extension archive needs, and every one of them asks the extractor to do something other than write a file.

cases.name: tar-gnu-longname-header-size-lie
cases.why: A GNU '@LongLink' ('L') metadata header declaring a size larger than the data behind it. TarReader reads a metadata header EAGERLY and raises InvalidOperationException — not InvalidDataException — which was not on the recognised-fault list, so the exception escaped Extract entirely AND the rollback (which sat on the non-throwing path) never ran: the innocent first member stayed on disk. The first member is here to prove the unwind, not for decoration.

cases.name: tar-gnu-longlink-header-size-lie
cases.why: The same lie in GNU's OTHER metadata header ('K', a long LINK name). Four header types carry a size the reader believes; a fix that only covered the one that was reported would leave three.

cases.name: tar-pax-extended-header-size-lie
cases.why: The pax per-entry extended-attributes header ('x') telling the same lie. .NET's own TarWriter emits one of these ahead of every pax entry, so this is the shape most likely to arrive in a real archive.

cases.name: tar-pax-global-header-size-lie
cases.why: The pax GLOBAL header ('g'). It is the one member type the extractor deliberately waves through without validating its name, which makes 'the reader trusts its declared size' worth pinning here rather than assuming it is covered by the per-entry case.

cases.name: tar-truncated-at-a-corrupt-header-cannot-be-detected
cases.why: An ACCEPT case that documents a limit rather than a capability, which is why it is worth a row. A tar's end is spelled by a zeroed header, so a header whose checksum field is zeroed is indistinguishable from the end of the archive — TarReader stops there and reports no error, and nothing downstream of it can tell 'the archive ended' from 'the archive was cut'. So `c.txt` is silently never extracted and the call reports success with one member written. `Succeeded` therefore means NOTHING WAS REFUSED, not EVERYTHING PRESENT WAS EXTRACTED; detecting a truncation needs an out-of-band manifest, which is the installer's obligation (#1941), not the extractor's. Pinned so the day the semantics change, it changes visibly.

cases.name: tar-benign
cases.why: The tar half of the must-still-work gate — including the leading `./` member `tar -cf x.tar .` emits, which denotes the destination root and must be a no-op rather than an error.
